newsitem.title: USA: U.S. report cites tobacco industry contributions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. report cites tobacco industry contributions.

text.p: Tobacco companies made hundreds of thousands of dollars in campaign contributions to members of Congress who opposed anti-smoking regulations, the Public Interest Research Group said in a report on Saturday.

The PIRG said the 124 House of Representatives members who signed a letter opposing federal regulations to reduce smoking by teen-agers received an average of $6,961 in campaign contributions from leading tobacco companies.
The 103 representatives who signed a letter supporting the regulations got an average of only $103 each, the group said.

Over a 10-year period, the 13 tobacco industry political action committees gave a total of $10.7 million in contributions to candidates for federal office, including $1.8 million from January, 1995 through June, 1996, the group said.

"This unprecedented flood of tobacco cash buys the industry pro-tobacco action by legislators and long-standing loyalty to this industry," William Novelli, president of the Campaign for Tobacco-Free Kids, said in a statement accompanying the report.

"We ask citizens across the country to tell their publicly-elected officials that our children are not for sale and to stop trading our kids' lives for tobacco cash," Novelli added. The campaign is a coalition of groups including the American Medical Association, the American Cancer Society and the National Parent-Teachers Association.
A report on Thursday by the Center for Responsive Politics found that Philip Morris led all political contributors in the past two years with a total of $2.74 million.

That included money to political action committees, which went mostly to congressional campaigns, as well as donations to national political parties, and large donations by PACs and individuals to the presidential campaigns of Republican Bob Dole and President Bill Clinton.

RJR Nabisco was seventh on the list which also included communications company AT&T, four labor unions, the American Medical Association, the Association of Trial Lawyers and the National Education Association.
